Small town: Senekal

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A town once known for unrest is now emerging as an unlikely rural film hub — not through major investment, but through volunteers with brooms, spades, and a quiet commitment to renewal.

Unique Selling Point:
After a tragedy that thrust it into the national spotlight, a small Free State town once defined by division is now quietly rewriting its story through community-led restoration, unexpected alliances, and a shared vision for the future.

Summary:
Senekal, nestled in the Eastern Free State, made news in 2020 for all the wrong reasons. The murder of 21-year-old Brendin Horner and the courthouse unrest that followed exposed deep social fault lines and simmering distrust. But in the months that followed, something extraordinary happened: people who once stood across from each other found a way to stand together.
At the heart of this transformation is the Senekal/Matwabeng Community Forum, born from a pastor’s quiet intervention. Farmers, township leaders, civic-minded youth, and local businesses joined forces to tackle the decay — potholes, parks, rubbish dumps, and fading hope.
Now, as streets are repaired and spaces renewed, filmmaker Frans Cronje has moved in, converting the old Sasko grain mill into a full-scale film studio. His vision: to turn Senekal into a rural production hub that builds local skills and jobs, with even PRASA now exploring a passenger rail link to support the initiative.


Further information:
Senekal is a small agricultural town nestled along the N5 in the Eastern Free State, framed by the wide, whispering grasslands that stretch endlessly toward the horizon. Known for its wheat, maize, and cattle, this is a place where the land gives generously — and where time moves with the pace of the seasons. At the heart of town stands the stately Dutch Reformed Church, encircled by something astonishing: a ring-wall built from fossilised tree trunks, dated back over 250 million years. Dug from the banks of the Sand River, these ancient sentinels surround the 250-year-old church like guardians of time — a symbol of endurance that echoes the spirit of Senekal itself.
But in October 2020, that enduring peace was shattered. The murder of young farm manager Brendin Horner became a flashpoint for national unrest. Protesters stormed the courthouse. A police van was set ablaze. And in a town where neighbours no longer looked each other in the eye, it felt like everything might fall apart. Then came the unexpected. A local pastor, armed not with policy but with presence, helped launch the Senekal/Matwabeng Community Forum — a space where township leaders, farmers, youth, and civic voices began to rebuild not just streets, but trust.
We return to the places that now carry new meaning: the train station, where township youth and farmers work together to scrub away years of neglect; the Sasko grain mill, now transforming into a rural film studio under the vision of filmmaker Frans Cronje; the restored swimming pool, abandoned for 33 years, now filled with life again. We’ll walk these spaces with those who made it happen — the pastor who held the first fragile conversations, the taxi boss who became an unlikely collaborator, the town’s oldest resident, whose memory stretches back across generations, and Cronje, who believes stories can plant economic roots as strong as any harvest.
Senekal isn’t just changing. It’s revealing what rural South Africa can become when division gives way to quiet, daily acts of courage — and when people decide that healing is their only way forward.
